text:
2 Start a new project







Task
Command




Create a project (only makes pyproject.toml)
uv init --bare


Choose the Python version (makes .python-version)
uv python pin 3.14


Add a package (updates pyproject.toml and uv.lock, builds .venv/)
uv add pandas


Add a specific version
uv add "pandas==3.1.1"


Add a package only needed for development, like testing
uv add --dev pytest


Remove a package
uv remove pandas




2.1 Make uv add write exact versions
By default uv add pandas writes "pandas>=3.1.1" (this version or newer) into pyproject.toml. For a data analysis project, add these lines to pyproject.toml so every uv add from now on writes an exact version ("pandas==3.1.1"):
[tool.uv]
add-bounds = "exact"
The setting only changes packages you add after it.

title: Makefile Cheatsheet
text:
A Makefile consists of rules that tell GNU Make how to build targets. Each rule follows this structure:
target : dependencies
    action
Example:
results/isles.dat : data/isles.txt scripts/wordcount.py
        python scripts/wordcount.py --input_file=data/isles.txt --output_file=results/isles.dat

Target: The name of the file(s) that will be created or updated.

Example: results/isles.dat

Dependencies: Files we need to build the target(s).

includes input files and scripts we will run to output the target(s)
Example: data/isles.txt scripts/wordcount.py
Targets can have 0 or more dependencies

Colon (:) separates targets from dependencies
Action: Commands to run to build or update the target using the dependencies.

Usually shell commands (e.g., running a Python script from command line)
Example: python scripts/wordcount.py --input_file=data/isles.txt --output_file=results/isles.dat
Targets can have zero or more actions

Comments: starting with #







NoteHigh bug zone: TAB required




Actions MUST be indented using the TAB, not spaces!
Depending on which computer you are using, sometimes TAB can still be auto-converted to 4 spaces if you are editing Makefile in VS Code or Jupyter Lab.
🍀 Safest choice: create and edit Makefile in command line using nano or vim from terminal.

title: Makefile Cheatsheet
text:
2.2 Step 2: Create a Makefile

TODO: Your task is to add a “smarter” data analysis pipeline using GNU Make! It should accomplish the same task as bash runall.sh when you type make all. It should also reset the analysis the starting point (the state when you first copied this repo) when you type make clean.

We will convert every commands in run_all.sh script into rules in Makefile.

2.2.1 First rule in Makefile

We start with converting the following command in run_all.sh script:

python scripts/wordcount.py --input_file=data/isles.txt --output_file=results/isles.dat

Create a new file called Makefile in the root directory:

nano Makefile

Add the following rule (pay attention to TAB indentation):

results/isles.dat : data/isles.txt scripts/wordcount.py
        python scripts/wordcount.py --input_file=data/isles.txt --output_file=results/isles.dat

Save the file above and run the make rule in the terminal:

make results/isles.dat






WarningDebug error: make: Nothing to be done for 'results/isles.dat'.





If you see the following output:
$ make results/isles.dat
make: Nothing to be done for `results/isles.dat'.
This means you are not using the correct TAB indentation. Try edit the Makefile in your terminal and redo all TAB key there.









WarningDebug message: make: 'results/isles.dat' is up to date.





If you succeed the first time you run the command above, but the second time you run the same command, it says:
$ make results/isles.dat
make: `results/isles.dat' is up to date.
This is normal, because your output file already exists, and the timestamp of that output file is more recent than the timestamp of the input file. Makefile will not re-run the command if you did not make any changes to the input file. If you update the timestamp of the input file using touch:
touch data/isles.txt
then rerun make results/isles.dat, it will run again, because now the timestamp of the input file is more recent than the timestamp of the output file, meaning that new changes have been made to the input file after you generated the output file last time.









TipQuestion: Can I call Makefile something else?





Yes you can, for example, if we call it random_name, you will just need to run the following command to generate the target output:
make -f random_name results/isles.dat





2.2.2 Create target and PHONY targets

It’s tedious to always type long file path & name, like results/isles.dat. You can create a target that is a short name for the long file path & name.

result : results/isles.dat

Usually we list those short names as PHONY targets, like this:

.PHONY : result
We use PHONY targets because:

It’s good practice to document and list all your target names in the begining of the Makefile.
If you have a file that is called the same name as a target, PHONY targets will tell GNU Make to ignore the file and use the target instead.


You can also add the clean target to delete everything:

clean:
    rm -f results/isles.dat

We update the Makefile to include new target, PHONY targets, clean target, and add a new rule to create the plot too:

.PHONY : result clean

result : results/isles.dat results/figure/isles.png

# count words
results/isles.dat : data/isles.txt scripts/wordcount.py
        python scripts/wordcount.py --input_file=data/isles.txt --output_file=results/isles.dat

# create the plots
results/figure/isles.png : results/isles.dat scripts/plotcount.py
        python scripts/plotcount.py \
                --input_file=results/isles.dat \
                --output_file=results/figure/isles.png

clean :
        rm -f results/isles.dat results/figure/isles.png

Test out our new Makefile!


Clean everything:

make clean

Would this run? Although we did not create results/isles.dat yet?

make results/figure/isles.png

🤩 Yes it will run! If GNU Make detects that you are missing the input file needed to create the target, it will try to find which rule can create this missing input file, and execute that rule first!
Clean everything again:

make clean

Run all the steps:

make result

# Makefile
# Tiffany Timbers, Nov 2018

# This driver script completes the textual analysis of
# 3 novels and creates figures on the 10 most frequently
# occuring words from each of the 3 novels. This script
# takes no arguments.

# example usage:
# make all

.PHONY: all dats figs clean-dats clean-figs clean-all

# run entire analysis
all: report/count_report.html

# count words
dats: results/isles.dat \
results/abyss.dat \
results/last.dat \
results/sierra.dat

results/isles.dat : scripts/wordcount.py data/isles.txt
    python scripts/wordcount.py \
        --input_file=data/isles.txt \
        --output_file=results/isles.dat
results/abyss.dat : scripts/wordcount.py data/abyss.txt
    python scripts/wordcount.py \
        --input_file=data/abyss.txt \
        --output_file=results/abyss.dat

    python scripts/wordcount.py \
        --input_file=data/last.txt \
        --output_file=results/last.dat
results/sierra.dat : scripts/wordcount.py data/sierra.txt
    python scripts/wordcount.py \
        --input_file=data/sierra.txt \
        --output_file=results/sierra.dat

# plot
figs : results/figure/isles.png \
    results/figure/abyss.png \
    results/figure/last.png \
    results/figure/sierra.png

results/figure/isles.png : scripts/plotcount.py results/isles.dat

        --input_file=results/isles.dat \
        --output_file=results/figure/isles.png
results/figure/abyss.png : scripts/plotcount.py results/abyss.dat

    results/figure/abyss.png \

    rm -rf report/count_report_files

2 Docker Compose

2.1 Why use Docker Compose?
We use docker-compose.yml file because it simplifies the process of typing complex docker run commands.


2.2 Basic Commands



Task
Command




Start docker container
docker compose up


Stop docker container
Ctrl + C (then docker compose rm)





2.3 Code we run in class: docker-compose.yml practice
Step-by-step instructions:

Please first cd to a local folder of your choice, don’t put all files in your home directory!

# Example `cd` command: 
cd /Users/skysheng/Desktop/github/dsci522

Make a new folder called demo_docker (or any other name you like)

mkdir demo_docker

Move into that folder we just created

cd demo_docker

Create a docker-compose.yml file using nano

nano docker-compose.yml

Copy and paste the following code into the docker-compose.yml file. Local port is set at 8789, password is set to password, username is rstudio.

services:
  analysis-env:
    image: rocker/rstudio:4.4.2
    ports:
      - "8789:8787"
    volumes:
      - .:/home/rstudio/project
    environment:
      PASSWORD: password
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 5G

You can also create this file using Graphical user interface (GUI) like VSCode.
If you used nano to create this file, you need to press Cntrl + X to attempt exit, by default it will ask you to save the file. Press Y and then press Enter to save the file.


Print out the content of the file to make sure it is correct.

cat docker-compose.yml

Launch the container using docker compose files.

docker compose up

After the container is launched, your terminal will be hanging. You can open your browser and go to http://localhost:8789 to access RStudio.
To stop the container, you need to type Cntrl + C in the terminal where you launched the container, and then type:

docker compose rm

title: Docker & Docker Compose Cheatsheet
text:
3 Dockerfile
A Dockerfile contains instructions for building a custom Docker image.
Basic structure:
# Start with a base image
FROM base_image:tag

# Copy files
COPY local_path container_path

# Run commands
RUN command

# Set environment variables
ENV VAR_NAME=value

3.1 Code we run in class: Dockerfile practice
We build an image that has our Python packages from uv.lock installed. We work like the textbook suggests: start small, build the image, try the next command inside the container, and only then add it to the Dockerfile.
Step-by-step instructions:

Please first cd to a local folder of your choice, don’t put all files in your home directory!

# Example `cd` command:
cd /Users/skysheng/Desktop/github/dsci522

Make a new folder called demo_docker (or any other name you like), and move into it

mkdir demo_docker
cd demo_docker

Create a uv project with one package. This makes pyproject.toml, .python-version and uv.lock (see the uv cheatsheet for what each file holds).

uv init --bare
uv python pin 3.14
uv add "pandas==3.1.1"

Print out the files to make sure they are correct.

cat pyproject.toml
cat .python-version

Create a Dockerfile using nano (or a GUI like VS Code).

nano Dockerfile

Copy and paste the following code into the Dockerfile. It starts from the official Python image (the same Python version as .python-version), copies the uv program into the image, and copies our three uv files into the folder /home/project.

FROM python:3.14-slim

COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/

WORKDIR /home/project
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./

If you used nano to create this file, you need to press Cntrl + X to attempt exit, by default it will ask you to save the file. Press Y and then press Enter to save the file.


Build the docker image locally:

# Build the docker image locally, with the tag name `testing_cmds`.
# pay attention to the dot at the end of the command!
docker build --tag testing_cmds .

Run the image you just built, and open a terminal inside the container:

docker run --rm -it testing_cmds bash

Inside the container, test the command that installs our packages, and check that it worked. --locked makes uv sync stop with an error if uv.lock does not match pyproject.toml.

uv sync --locked
uv run python -c "import pandas; print(pandas.__version__)"

If the above commands work, exit the container by typing exit.
Update the Dockerfile to include the newly tested command. We also tell uv to put the environment in /opt/venv instead of /home/project/.venv, so it is not hidden when we later mount our project folder over /home/project, and we put /opt/venv/bin first on the PATH, so python means the environment’s Python.

FROM python:3.14-slim

COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/

WORKDIR /home/project

ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./
RUN uv sync --locked
ENV PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH"

Re-build the docker image (same command as step 7), then check that pandas is installed:

docker build --tag testing_cmds .
docker run --rm testing_cmds python -c "import pandas; print(pandas.__version__)"

Iterate through steps 7 to 12 (build the image, run the container’s terminal, test a new command, add it to the Dockerfile, build again …) until you are happy with your Dockerfile.
Use the image with your project folder mounted, so the container can see your files:

docker run --rm -it -v "/$(pwd)":/home/project testing_cmds bash






TipAdding a package later



Add it on your computer with uv add <package>, which updates pyproject.toml and uv.lock, then rebuild the image (step 7).

cp -r folder1 folder2 — Copy folder recursively

title: Linux Command Line Cheatsheet
text:
7 Permissions & Ownership

chmod 400 key.pem — Change file permission

first digit = privillage of owner of the file; second digit = other people in the same group; third digit = everyone else in the world
4 = read, 2 = write, 1 = execute

7 = 4 + 2 + 1 = read & write & execute
Examples:

400 = read-only by owner

600 = read/write by owner

756 = full access for owner, read & execute for others in the same group, read & write for everyone else in the world


chown user:group folder/ — Change ownership of the folder
sudo — Run command with superuser privileges, “super user do”

title: Teamwork Contract
text:
How to use the template

Create a file named team-contract.qmd. The contract is fairly personal, so it does not need to be in your public project repository.
Copy the template below (the button at the top right of the block copies it) and paste it into team-contract.qmd.
Replace everything in [square brackets]. The template is a starting point, not a form: change, add or remove anything so it describes how your team will work. Talk it through as a team before you write it down. A contract that is mostly the template with the brackets filled in will lose marks. See Milestone 1 for what a contract could cover.

quarto render team-contract.qmd
This creates team-contract.pdf next to it. The template uses Quarto’s built-in Typst format, so you do not need LaTeX installed.

title: Teamwork Contract
text:
Template
---
title: "Team contract"
subtitle: "DSCI 522, group [NUMBER]"
author:
  - "[TEAM MEMBER 1]"
  - "[TEAM MEMBER 2]"
  - "[TEAM MEMBER 3]"
  - "[TEAM MEMBER 4]" # delete this line for a team of three
date: today
format: typst
---

## Expectations

The time expected for group members to work on DSCI 522
will be a maximum of [NUMBER] hours a week,
unless all the team members agree to lengthen the time expected.
If team members cannot complete their sections within the maximum hours,
members should give notice on Slack at least 24 hours before the group submission deadline
to see if work should be redistributed or if the expected time should be increased.

All submissions are expected to meet the criteria of the milestones
as set out in the instructions.
This includes making sure all scripts are working,
creating tests for all our functions,
and using proper grammar in written submissions.

## Work distribution

At each weekly meeting, we will split the milestone into small tasks,
open a GitHub issue for each one, and assign it to a team member.
Over the course, everyone should do a similar amount of
coding, writing, and reviewing.
[DESCRIBE HOW YOUR TEAM WILL MAKE SURE THE WORK STAYS FAIR,
E.G., ROTATING WHO WRITES CODE VS. WHO WRITES THE REPORT.]

## Availability

Team members are not available at the following times:

- [TEAM MEMBER 1]: [E.G., EVENINGS AFTER 8 PM, SUNDAYS]
- [TEAM MEMBER 2]: [...]
- [TEAM MEMBER 3]: [...]
- [TEAM MEMBER 4]: [...]

We will not expect replies or reviews from someone during their unavailable times.

## Meetings

Meeting times were established during the initial team meeting held on [DATE].
Meetings will be held [PLACE, OR ONLINE ON ...] at the following times:

- [DAY]: [TIME]
- [DAY]: [TIME] (if needed)

The group will have a second formal meeting during the DSCI 522 lab on [DAY] at [TIME].
All members are expected to attend the meetings.
If a member cannot make a meeting,
written notice must be given 24 hours before the meeting to discuss alternative options.

## Communication

All project discussion outside of meetings will happen in GitHub issues:
ideas, suggestions, decisions, splitting up tasks, and meeting notes.
Work is submitted and reviewed through pull requests.
Slack is only for scheduling meetings and quick informal messages.
If an important decision is made on Slack, we will record it in a GitHub issue.

## Reviews

All members are expected to submit a pull request for their work
on the group project's repository on GitHub.com.
Members are expected to add teammates as reviewers,
so that every pull request is reviewed by another teammate.
Pull requests should be reviewed within [NUMBER] hours after creation.

## Use of AI

[DESCRIBE IF AND HOW YOUR TEAM WILL USE GENERATIVE AI (E.G., CHATGPT, CLAUDE, COPILOT),
AND FOR WHAT KINDS OF TASKS.]
Every team member is responsible for understanding and checking
any code or text they submit, whether or not AI helped write it.
Pull requests and GitHub issues are opened by team members, never by an AI agent or chat bot.
We may use AI agents to help double-check the code before merging pull requests,
but ultimately it is human reviewers who make the final decisions and merge the pull requests.
We will keep track of how we use AI so we can write the AI use statement in our README.

## Roles

There are two roles team members will be responsible for each week:

1. Scribe:
    - Responsible for taking notes at the meetings and in-class lab sessions,
      and adding them as a GitHub issue.
    - Responsible for sharing all notes and in-class activities with teammates.
2. Proof-reader:
    - Responsible for doing a final check of the submission before the deadline,
      to make sure all requirements are satisfied.

Roles will be rotated each week, so that each team member does each role at least once.

## Deadlines

Deadlines for individual items will be assigned during meetings.
The proof-reader will review the work on [DAY]
and ensure that the final version is ready for submission,
and will create the required GitHub release.

## Breach of contract

Failure to follow the team contract will result in a three-step warning system:

1. A written Slack notice that outlines the violation of the team contract
   and reminds the member of the team contract's conditions.
2. A meeting to discuss the behaviour,
   after which the member writes an agreement to follow the team contract.
3. Reaching out to the lab instructor or TAs about the issues with the teammate.

section: 1. Create a Makefile to act as a driver script to rule them all
text:
1. Create a Makefile to act as a driver script to rule them all
This script should run the others in sequence, hard coding in the appropriate arguments. This script should:

live in the project’s root directory and be named Makefile
be well documented (using the project README and comments inside the Makefile to explain what it does and how to use it)
have an all target so that you can easily run the entire analysis from top to bottom by running make all at the command line
have a clean target so that you can easily “undo” your analysis by running make clean at the command line (e.g., deletes all generated data and files).
have a publish target that updates the copy of your report that GitHub Pages publishes (docs/index.html, from Milestone 2). make publish replaces the steps you did by hand in Milestone 2. make all should run it too, so your published report never falls behind your analysis. Commit and push docs/ after it runs.







NotePhony targets




The all, clean and publish targets may be .PHONY targets
You can create other targets that link up all the dependencies

For example, data, analysis, figures, pdf, etc, so your build process only runs what’s necessary during development
Your other targets should be using make dependencies, i.e., not all your targets are allowed to be phony targets.




For example, publish can be a phony target that depends on the real file docs/index.html. Change the report’s path to your own:


Makefile

publish: docs/index.html

docs/index.html: reports/<your-report>.html
    mkdir -p docs
    cp reports/<your-report>.html docs/index.html
    touch docs/.nojekyll

Because docs/index.html depends on your rendered report, make publish copies it only when the report has changed.

title: Milestone 4
section: 2. Abstract some code from your scripts to functions in a separate file, and write tests for those functions
text:
2. Abstract some code from your scripts to functions in a separate file, and write tests for those functions
In every data science project, there is some code that is repetitive, and other code that may not be repetitive in the current project, but would likely be very useful in other, related future projects. It is well worth it to abstract such code to functions, making it easily reuseable in the future in other work. Examples of code that often repetitive in a data analysis projects:

data wrangling, cleaning or transformation code that gets applied to multiple columns or multiple data sets
data visualization code when many versions of a similar plot-type is used (e.g., many scatter plots with similar formatting)
data modeling workflow/pipeline code when tuning different models on the same data set

Abstracting our analysis code into functions also makes it testable! Meaning you can assess whether your code works as expected. This alone is reason enough to use functions in your analysis code.
Your job here is to create at least one function per group member from your scripts. When doing this task, follow the workflow for writing functions and tests for data science, remember this process will include:

writing thorough function specifications & documentation
writing robust unit tests for these functions to ensure they work as expected
writing the code that makes up the function body

If you are using Python, these functions will live in an .py file (whose filename will be named after the function, or functions). Again, it is OK to have one function per file, or all functions in one file. This/these file(s) will live in a sub-directory called src. If you are using R, these functions will live in an .R file (whose filename will be named after the function, or functions). It is OK to have one function per file, or all functions in one file. This/these file(s) will live in a sub-directory called R.
You will import (in the case of Python) or source (in the case of R) these functions in your scripts to use them in your analysis. Tests will live in a test directory, with files/subdirectories organized as per the testing framework you are using. If you are using Python, we expect you to use the pytest Python package framework. If you are using R for your data analysis code, we expect you to use the testthat R package framework for writing software tests.
Of course, if it makes sense to have more than one function per group member, you are welcome to increase the number! However, all functions must have the same standards in regards to software robustness. Your functions will be assessed for their quality (e.g., functions should do one thing, and generally return an object unless they were specifically designed for side-effects), usability, readability (follow the black style guide for Python, or the tidyverse style guide for R), documentation and quality of the test suite.

Milestone 2 summary

Upgrade your project’s computational environment to a container.
Publish your report on GitHub Pages.

An example Milestone 2 that corresponds to our expectations from this year is here: Breast Cancer Predictor in Python 1.0.0
 ### 0. Repository transfer
The owner of your group’s repository will transfer their repository into the MDS 2025-25 org: https://github.ubc.ca/MDS-2025-26/.
You can do this in the repositroy settings. Make sure everyone else in the group has filled out the GitHub username survey. 
You are no longer transfering the repository for this course, so we will just have to track your individual repos during assignment submission.

1. Use a container for the computational environment
Write a Dockerfile to create a custom container for the computational environment for your project. Build your container using GitHub Actions, and publish your container image on DockerHub. Once this is done, shift the development of your project from working in a virtual environment to working in a container!
The Dockerfile is the file used to specify and create the Docker image from which containers can be run to create an reproducible computational environment for your analysis. For this project, we recommend using a base Docker image that already has most of the software dependencies needed for your analysis. In particular, the quay.io/jupyter/minimal-notebook image. When you add other software dependencies to this Dockerfile, ensure that you pin the version of the software that you add. You can do this most easily if you use our recommended environment.yml > conda-lock.yml > Dockerfile workflow that you learned about in individual_assignment2.
Note - this document should live in the root of your public GitHub.com repository.
In this milestone, we expect you to add a GitHub Actions workflow to automatically build the image, push it to DockerHub, and version the image (using latest is okay for now) and GitHub repo when changes are pushed to the Dockerfile
You will need to add your DockerHub username and password (naming them DOCKER_USERNAME and DOCKER_PASSWORD, respectively) as GitHub secrets to this repository for this to work. This part is similar to Individual Assignment 3.
Additionally, document how to use and update your container image in your README. This is important to make it easy for you and your team to shift to a container solution for your computational environment. We also expect you will use Docker Compose so that launching your containers is as frictionless as possible (which makes you more likely to use this tool in your workflow)!






ImportantYour README instructions are worth 5 all-or-nothing points



5 points of this milestone are for the reproducibility of your README instructions: whether someone can follow them to launch your container and run your analysis in it. These points are all-or-nothing. If your instructions do not work exactly as you have written them, you will lose all 5 points.
Make sure your instructions work on both Windows and Mac computers. If your team does not have both, work with another team to test them.




2. Publish your report on GitHub Pages
Anyone should be able to read your report online, without cloning your repository. You learned to publish with GitHub Pages in DSCI 521 (Introduction to Quarto and GitHub Pages), where you published a whole Quarto website. Here you apply those skills to publish the HTML version of your report.






NoteAlready published your report in Milestone 1?



Switch to the setup below, even if your current one works. Later milestones build on it.


You publish by hand, with a small workaround. It works because of how GitHub Pages serves files:

GitHub Pages can publish the files in a docs/ folder on your main branch, exactly as they are.
When someone visits your site’s address, the web server shows the file named index.html.
With embed-resources: true, your rendered report is a single HTML file that holds everything it needs, including its figures.

So publishing your report is just putting a copy of that one file at docs/index.html. Copying files by hand is easy to forget, so it is not how you would publish a larger site. Later in the program (in DSCI 524, when you build websites for your packages), you will use tools that build and publish a website for you.

Make your rendered report a single, self-contained HTML file, with embed-resources: true in its HTML options, for example in the report’s YAML header:
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
If your project’s _quarto.yml already sets this, you don’t need to add it again. A self-contained file holds its figures and styling, so it still works after you copy it somewhere else. If you have only been rendering your report to PDF, render it to HTML as well.
Render your report. Then copy the rendered HTML file into a docs/ folder at the root of your repository, and name the copy index.html:
mkdir -p docs
cp <path-to-your-report>.html docs/index.html
Add an empty .nojekyll file to docs/, so that GitHub Pages serves your file exactly as it is (see Turning off Jekyll with .nojekyll):
touch docs/.nojekyll
Commit and push docs/. It is a copy of a generated file, but GitHub Pages can only publish files that are in your repository. Check that your .gitignore does not ignore docs/ or .html files.
In your repository on GitHub.com, go to Settings > Pages. Under Build and deployment, choose Deploy from a branch, then the main branch and the /docs folder, and click Save.
After a few minutes, your report is published at https://ubc-mds-2026-27.github.io/<your-repository>/. Open it and check that the whole report shows, including its figures.
Put this URL in your README (as the link to your rendered report) and in the About section of your repository.







ImportantKeep the published report up to date



docs/index.html is a copy. Each time you re-render your report, copy it into docs/ again and push, or the published version will fall behind. We grade your work from your 1.0.0 release, and the report on GitHub Pages should match it.

title: Bonus: Project website
section: 1. Turn your project into a website
text:
1. Turn your project into a website
Your project’s _quarto.yml, in the root of your repository, already tells Quarto how to render your report. Turn it into a website’s configuration: add type: website and output-dir: docs, list the website’s pages in render, and add a website section with the menu bar. Keep the format settings you already have (for example, embed-resources and the PDF settings): they still apply to your report.
Here is a starting point. Change the title, the report’s file name and the repository URL to your own:


_quarto.yml

project:
  type: website
  output-dir: docs
  render:
    - index.qmd
    - about.qmd
    - reports/<your-report>.qmd

website:
  title: "Your project title"
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - href: reports/<your-report>.qmd
        text: Report
      - href: about.qmd
        text: About
    right:
      - icon: github
        href: https://github.com/UBC-MDS-2026-27/<your-repository>
        aria-label: GitHub repository

# Keep your existing `format:` settings below.

The render list keeps files like CONTRIBUTING.md out of the website. Give each new page format: html in its YAML header, so that Quarto does not also make a PDF of it when your project renders your report to PDF.
As in the DSCI 521 chapter, create an empty .nojekyll file in the root of your repository (see Turning off Jekyll with .nojekyll). Quarto copies it into docs/ every time you render. Add .quarto/ to your .gitignore if it is not there already.
Your repository will look something like this (only the new and changed parts are shown):
.
├── _quarto.yml           # now a website: renders everything into docs/
├── .nojekyll
├── Makefile
├── README.md
├── index.qmd             # homepage: includes README.md
├── about.qmd             # the team
├── reports/
│   └── <your-report>.qmd
└── docs/                 # the published website (generated, but committed)
    ├── index.html
    └── reports/
        ├── <your-report>.html
        └── <your-report>.pdf






ImportantYour report now renders into docs/



Your report is now a page of the website. Quarto writes it to docs/reports/<your-report>.html and .pdf, with the website’s menu bar, instead of next to the .qmd in reports/. Delete the old rendered files from reports/, and update your Makefile and README to the new locations. This bonus is graded from the same 3.0.0 release as Milestone 4, so your Milestone 4 README instructions must still work exactly as written.


quarto render now renders the whole website. To render just your report while you work on it, quarto render reports/<your-report>.qmd still works, and quarto preview shows the website as you edit it.

title: Bonus: Project website
section: 2. The homepage, the about page and the report
text:
2. The homepage, the about page and the report

The homepage (index.qmd)
Your README already says what your project is, who made it, and how to run it, so make it your homepage. index.qmd only needs to include it, using Quarto’s include shortcode:


index.qmd

---
format: html
---

{{< include README.md >}}

You don’t need a title: Quarto uses the first heading of your README as the page title. Including the file, rather than copying it, means the homepage stays up to date whenever your README changes.






WarningLinks in your README must work on the website too



The website only publishes its pages, not the rest of your repository. A relative link in your README to a file such as CONTRIBUTING.md, LICENSE.md or src/ works on GitHub but is broken on the website, and Quarto does not warn you about it. Link to those files with their full GitHub URL instead (for example, https://github.com/UBC-MDS-2026-27/<your-repository>/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md), which works in both places.




The about page (about.qmd)
The about page lists and introduces each member of your team. For each person, include:

their name, linked to their GitHub profile
a few sentences introducing them, in their own words (for example, their background before MDS and what interests them in data science)

Your website is public, so each person decides what they share about themselves. A photo is optional.


The report
The menu bar’s Report item links to reports/<your-report>.qmd, and Quarto turns that into a link to the rendered page. When your report also renders to PDF, Quarto adds a link to the PDF version on the report’s page. Link to both versions from your README too, so they show up on the homepage.
Every figure in your report and on your website needs alt text: a short description of what the figure shows, for readers who cannot see it. Use the fig-alt option on code cells that make figures, and the fig-alt attribute on images:
![Feature densities.](../results/figures/densities.png){#fig-densities fig-alt="Density plots of each feature by class."}
See Alt text in the Quarto documentation.

title: Bonus: Project website
text:
3. One make command builds everything
Your Makefile from Milestone 4 already runs your analysis. Extend it so that make all, run from a fresh clone inside your container, does everything, in order:

downloads the data
runs your data validation checks
runs the rest of your analysis
publishes: renders the website, including your report, into docs/

make clean should remove everything that make all creates, including docs/.
In Milestone 4, your publish target copied your report to docs/index.html, and make all ran it. For the bonus, change the rule behind publish so that it renders the website instead, and remove your old rule for the report in reports/: the report now renders as part of the website. Here is a sketch. Change the file names to your own, and list as prerequisites every file the website reads, including your README and the figures and tables your report shows, so make rebuilds the website when one of them changes:


Makefile

.DELETE_ON_ERROR:

publish: docs/index.html

docs/index.html: _quarto.yml index.qmd README.md about.qmd \
        reports/<your-report>.qmd results/figures/<your-figure>.png
    quarto render

clean:
    rm -rf docs
    # ... and everything else your pipeline creates

quarto render empties docs/ before it renders, so no pages are left over from an older version of the website. .DELETE_ON_ERROR: makes make delete docs/index.html if the render fails partway. Without it, the next make would find a docs/index.html and say there is nothing to do.






ImportantA clean build, with no warnings



Before you submit, run make clean and then make all inside your container. Everything should rebuild, and Quarto should print no ERROR or WARN messages (for example, about links it could not find). Messages from other tools, such as Jupyter, don’t count. We will grade this bonus by doing the same.


Update your README to say how to build the website.

Policies

Academic Integrity
Academic integrity is a commitment to honesty, respect, responsibility, and accountability in academic work. It is foundational to teaching and learning and is a shared value of all members of the UBC community. In a project course, it also means being transparent with your teammates and the teaching team about how your work was produced.
Academic integrity in this course includes:

Submitting individual assignments that reflect your own understanding and intellectual contribution.
Contributing your fair share to your group’s project, and making sure your commits, pull requests, and reviews honestly represent the work you did.
Citing any code, text, or ideas you draw on from elsewhere (classmates outside your group, documentation, Stack Overflow, blog posts, generative AI tools, etc.), following the MDS program policy.
Respecting the licenses of any code, data, or other material you reuse in your project.
Following the generative AI policy below, including disclosing AI use for every deliverable.



Use of Generative AI
This course follows the MDS program’s Academic Integrity and Use of Generative AI policy. Assessment-specific instructions always take precedence over the general guidance below.
AI assistance is allowed. Generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, GitHub Copilot, Cursor) are a real part of modern data science workflows, and you may use them in this course to brainstorm, explain concepts, debug errors, or help write code and documentation. That said, this course is about building your own skills in version control, environments, containers, testing, and pipelines. We strongly encourage you to attempt the work yourself first, and to use AI to support your learning rather than replace it. A useful question to ask yourself is: is this tool helping me understand the problem, or is it doing the thinking I am here to learn to do?
Disclose your AI use. For every milestone and individual assignment, you must state whether generative AI was used, including when it was not. If AI was used, please share:

which tool(s) and model(s) you used;
which parts of the work they were used for, and how; and
the instructions you gave the tool, such as any system prompt or agent configuration file (e.g., CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .cursor/rules/, .github/copilot-instructions.md), or, if you did not use one, a few representative example prompts.

For group milestones, please keep this disclosure in an AI_USAGE.md file or CLAUDE.md (or other file names that indicate AI was used) in the root of your project repository and update it as the project evolves. For individual assignments, include the disclosure with your Gradescope submission. Disclosing AI use is not penalized, and it helps us give you useful feedback.
You remain responsible for everything you submit. Whether code was written by you, a teammate, or an AI tool, everyone in the group is responsible for its correctness, quality, and licensing. You should be able to explain what your code does, why it is designed that way, and how it fits into the rest of your project. Please do not merge code you have not read and understood.
Humans open pull requests and issues, and make the final merge decisions. Importantgithub.com not https://github.ubc.ca/



Make sure you do this in your own personal public GitHub account. Do not make this in the UBC github.



Clone your learning-about-version-control repository to your local computer.
Create and resolve a merge conflict 😱!

On GitHub.com, open your README.md, click the pencil (edit) icon, and add a line that says “Solving merge conflicts is easy!”. Commit the change on GitHub.
On your local computer (without pulling first!), add a line in the same place in the README, but this time write “Solving merge conflicts is soooooo hard!”
Add and commit your local changes to the README.md, then try to push. Git will reject the push, because GitHub has a commit you don’t have locally yet.
Pull the changes from GitHub with git pull --no-rebase. This is when the merge conflict appears. (The --no-rebase tells git to merge the two versions. Without it, newer versions of git stop and ask you how to combine them.)
Resolve the merge conflict on your local computer so that the line reads “Solving merge conflicts takes conscious effort, but I can do it!”. Take a screenshot while you are resolving the conflict (with the conflict markers <<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>> visible) to show you did this.
Add and commit the resolved file, then push to your remote repository on GitHub.com.

Create and accept a pull request!

Add and commit your changes to local version control.
Push the changes to the README.md that you made on the opinions branch to the remote repository on GitHub.com.

Merge the pull request you opened, so your changes from the opinions branch go into the main branch.

The purpose of this assignment is to ensure that everyone gains hands-on practice creating reproducible reports using Quarto.
Throughout the pre-requisites for DSCI 522, you have become familiar with using Jupyter Notebooks to interweave narration and runnable code into a single document. This allowed you to pass your analysis over to a co-worker or reviewer, who could reproduce your work by running your notebook from top to bottom.
But is Jupyter Notebook the best we can do to create reproducible data analysis? Not entirely… For example, Jupyter Notebooks struggle with organization and configuration. Imagine you have an extremely long and complicated report packed into a single Jupyter Notebook. Writing out a table of contents, formatting a bibliography, and adding labels to figures can become extremely cumbersome, especially as they evolve with your analysis during the review process.
Imagine you have 25 figures and tables labelled 1 to 25 and you decide to add a new figure at the very start of your report; figure 1 now needs to be renamed to figure 2, table 2 now needs to be renamed to table 3, figure 3 now needs to be renamed to figure 4…
This is where Quarto (and related tools) can come in handy. Although they have their own set of disadvantages, they are certainly an improvement over plain Jupyter Notebooks. They allow for the automatic creation and formatting of a table of contents, a bibliography, and those pesky figure labels, among many other features. During this individual assignment, you will start to familiarize yourself with Quarto reports, start to understand their advantages and disadvantages, and begin to recognize their similarities and differences from basic Jupyter notebooks.

title: Milestone 1
text:
Milestone 1 summary
In this milestone, you will:

Draft a teamwork contract
Set up a public GitHub repository in the course organization, with its required metadata
Create an appropriate file and directory structure for a data analysis project
Write the data analysis as a Quarto document (.qmd)
Make the computational environment reproducible with a virtual environment (uv or renv). Hint: do this as you create the analysis, don’t wait until the end!

An example Milestone 1 that corresponds to our expectations from this year is here: Breast Cancer Predictor in Python 0.0.1

1. Draft a teamwork contract
This document will govern the working relationships on your team, and if done correctly, it should help you manage and resolve any issues that might arise when working in a group. Start from the teamwork contract template, based on a contract from a past data science project: copy it into a Quarto document, make it your team’s own, and render it to PDF.
A teamwork contract communicates how the group will work together. It includes details about the logistics of working together, the expectations you have for each other, and how you plan to navigate conflicts.
Some aspects of the teamwork contract could be:

How will work be distributed in a fair and equitable way?
What are the expected work hours for the project?
How often will group meetings occur?
Will you have meeting agendas and minutes? If so, what will be the system for rotating through these responsibilities?
What will be the style of working?

Will you start each day with stand-ups, or submit a summary of your contributions 4 hours before each meeting? or something else?

What is the quality of work each team member expects from themselves and each other?
When are team members not available (e.g., evenings and Sundays because of family obligations).
And any other similar things that govern your working relationships.

Use this opportunity to use your prior knowledge/experience to improve your teamwork, communication, leadership, and organizational skills. You will need all of these for your capstone projects (and beyond)! Please actually talk this through as a team and fill it in with care. A contract that is clearly rushed or left mostly as the template will lose marks.

Note - this document is fairly personal and does NOT need to reside in your public GitHub.com repo. Instead you can prove that you created this by submitting a copy of it to Gradescope under the Milestone 1 assignment.



2. Set up a GitHub repository
After we add you to the UBC-MDS-2026-27 organization on GitHub.com, set up a public GitHub repository for your group under that organization (not under one of your personal accounts), and give your whole team access to it (see Repository metadata below). Once you have decided on a project question and data set, make sure your repository has a name that is relevant to that question. Note: if you need to change the name of your project repository later, you can!
We are using github.com and public repositories because we will eventually be using some fancy tooling (e.g., GitHub Actions) in this project. For this to work, all your work for this project (including scripts) should be developed and live in this repository on GitHub.com. Additionally, this will help you build a portfolio of your work you can share with others.

Repository metadata






ImportantThis metadata is used for the class automatons, and it is also worth points



Proper metadata setup is also graded, on top of the rest of this milestone. Metadata that is not fixed in week 1 (by the Milestone 1 deadline) will continue to lose points in each milestone until it is fixed.
Lab attendance is mandatory, and the teaching team is there with you. There is no reason for a username or metadata problem to be left unresolved, or at least undocumented, after your week 1 lab session.


Your group’s repository needs all three of the following:

It lives in the course organization. Create it in UBC-MDS-2026-27, not under a personal account or the UBC-MDS organization.
Its Description begins with DSCI 522. It must be literally these characters: capital DSCI, one space, 522, at the very start of the description. The rest of the description is up to your group; use it to say what your project is about. To edit it, click the gear icon next to About on your repository’s main page.

Correct: DSCI 522: Predicting wine quality from its chemistry
Incorrect: dsci 522 ..., DSCI522 ..., DSCI-522 ..., Predicting wine quality (DSCI 522), or a description with a space before DSCI 522

3. Create an appropriate file & directory structure for a data analysis project
For this project, you are expected to follow the best practices we have learned about in regards to project directory and file structures. For this milestone, your repository should look something like this. Include whichever of these files are relevant to your project: for example, the uv files if you use Python, the renv files if you use R, or both if you use both.
your-project-name/
├── README.md
├── CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md
├── CONTRIBUTING.md
├── LICENSE.md
├── .gitignore
├── pyproject.toml          # Python (uv)
├── uv.lock                 # Python (uv)
├── .python-version         # Python (uv)
├── renv.lock               # R (renv)
├── .Rprofile               # R (renv)
├── renv/                   # R (renv): follow the .gitignore in here
├── data/
│   ├── raw/                # data exactly as downloaded
│   └── processed/          # cleaned / intermediate data
└── analysis/               # or reports/, src/
    ├── <descriptive-name>.qmd
    └── <descriptive-name>.html  # or .pdf
Keep the project root tidy: only the files above that are relevant to your project should live there. Put the analysis document in a sub-folder with a sensible name (e.g., analysis/, reports/), not in the root. Too many files in the root makes it hard for collaborators (including future you!) to find things.
Add a .gitignore so that system and temporary files never get committed. At minimum, it should ignore .DS_Store and .venv/.
The description of each file and folder follows.

i. README.md
The README.md lives in the root of your repository. It is the first thing people see, so it should tell a stranger what this project is and how to run it. Include:

Project title that matches your project topic.
Authors: the names of all team members.
Summary: a short paragraph (view from 10,000 feet) that says what question you asked, what you found at a high level, and 1-2 sentences on what the findings might mean.
How to run the analysis: step-by-step instructions that someone who has never seen your project can follow, from cloning the repo to rendering the report. Tell them how to set up the environment (e.g., uv sync) and which command to run. Don’t make the reader guess.
Dependencies: list them (e.g., uv, Quarto) or link to where they are listed (e.g., pyproject.toml).
Licenses: the names of the licenses in LICENSE.md (e.g., MIT and CC BY-NC-ND 4.0).
AI use statement: say whether you used generative AI (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot) in this project. If you did, say how. If you used instruction files (e.g., CLAUDE.md, a system prompt file), commit them to the repo and point to them. Also include a few example prompts.
Link to the rendered report (e.g., your GitHub Pages URL).

Click every link in your README to make sure it works, and proofread for spelling and grammar.


ii. CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md
In an attempt to create a safe, positive, productive, and happy community, many organizations and developers create a code of conduct for their projects. A code of conduct in a Data Science project informs others of social norms, acceptable behaviour and general etiquette. It is more outward facing than the teamwork contract discussed above. We recommend Project Include for a comprehensive guide to writing an effective Code of Conduct.
At minimum, we believe that a good/effective code of conduct should include:

A statement on diversity and inclusivity
Details on expected, and unacceptable behaviour
A list of consequences for unacceptable behaviour
A procedure for reporting and dealing with unacceptable behaviour

It is fine to adapt an existing code of conduct, but you must cite the original source (its name and a link) in the file. If you adapt one, update the contact email in the reporting/enforcement section so it reaches your team, not the original project. Proofread it.

Sample Codes of Conduct:

idocde Coc
Python Community CoC
Tidyverse CoC
Pandas CoC
Vox Media CoC

Note - this document should live in the root of your public GitHub.com repository.



iii. CONTRIBUTING.md
It is a good practice to include information about how others, outside the core team, can contribute to your project somewhere in your repository. This is typically done as a separate file in the repository called CONTRIBUTING.md. After reading it, someone should know how to report a bug, suggest a change, and submit their work (e.g., open an issue, make a branch, open a pull request). Here are some examples of this file:

Altair
dplyr
Atom editor (very comprehensive)
AI fairness research paper

Your CONTRIBUTING.md is also required to have an AI policy section. It tells contributors whether and how they may use generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Copilot, Claude) when they contribute to your project: what is allowed, what they must disclose, and who is responsible for the result. Your policy must be consistent with this course’s expectations (see Expectations: pull requests and issues are opened, reviewed and merged by you, not by an AI agent). Here are some examples of AI policies from open source projects:

earthaccess
SciPy
SymPy

Same rule as the code of conduct: if you adapt any of these, cite the original source. Fill in every section (no leftover template placeholders) and check that all links work.
Note - this document should live in the root of your public GitHub.com repository.


iv. data/
The data/ folder should contain a copy of the downloaded data, and it should get written there by code in your analysis (not downloaded by hand). Keep raw data and processed data separate: put the data exactly as you downloaded it in data/raw/, and anything you clean or create from it in data/processed/.
An exception can be made if the data set is extremely large (> 100 MB per file). In that case, reach out to the instructional team to make an alternative plan, and explain in your README why the data is not in the repo.


v. analysis/<descriptive-name>.qmd
For this milestone, the analysis code and narration should be contained within a single Quarto document (.qmd). See section 4 for what goes inside it. A few rules for the file itself:

Put it in a sub-folder (e.g., analysis/), not the project root.
Give it a descriptive name related to your project (e.g., penguin-species-classification.qmd), not analysis.qmd.
Push both the source document AND the rendered version (HTML or PDF). If you render to HTML, set up GitHub Pages so the report is easy to read online, and put its URL in your README.
Keep only one report. Delete drafts and scratch files so it is obvious which document is the real one.
Make sure it renders without errors.



vi. pyproject.toml, uv.lock & .python-version (or the corresponding renv files)
These files let others recreate your computational environment. See section 5 for details.
Note - these files should live in the root of your public GitHub.com repository.


vii. LICENSE.md
Licenses tell others how they may (or may not) use your work. We will learn more about licenses later in the course, and for now we recommend using an MIT license for the project code and a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0) license for the project report. As long as your group agrees, these can be changed later in the course when you learn more about licenses. If you want to spend some time choosing different licenses now, we can recommend these two websites to help get you started:

https://choosealicense.com/
https://chooser-beta.creativecommons.org/

Your LICENSE.md needs:

Two licenses: one software license for the code (e.g., MIT) and one Creative Commons license for the report (e.g., CC BY-NC-ND 4.0).
The actual license text pasted into the file, not just a link to it.
The names of all team members in the copyright line.

The licenses named in your README should match the ones in LICENSE.md. Name the file exactly LICENSE.md.



4. Write the data analysis as a Quarto document
The content of this analysis project should be a narrated analysis that asks and answers a predictive or inferential question using a method you have already learned in MDS. For milestone 1, the code and analysis narrative should be contained within a single Quarto document (.qmd), using either Python or R code chunks.
Write it like a short scientific report. Your report should have the following sections:

Title
Summary: one paragraph that says what question you asked, what you found, and why it matters, plus the main limitations.
Introduction:

give enough background on the topic that someone unfamiliar with it can follow the rest of your report
explain why this problem is important or interesting. Don’t stop at one sentence; convince the reader it is worth answering.
clearly state the question you are trying to answer
describe the data set you used: where it comes from, what each row is, and which variables you use. Cite the data set.
clearly define your target/response variable (what you are predicting)
make sure your question can actually be answered with this data

Methods:

in written English, walk the reader through what you did from beginning to end, and why
name the model or method you used and explain why it fits your question
name the metric you used to evaluate it (e.g., accuracy, F1, RMSE) and explain why you chose it
your report should include code which:

downloads the data from its original source on the web and saves a copy to data/raw/
wrangles and cleans the data from its original (downloaded) format to the format needed for your analysis, and saves it to data/processed/
splits the data into training and test sets before doing any exploratory data analysis or preprocessing. Don’t break the golden rule of machine learning: the test set should not influence any decision you make.
summarizes the training data in a way that is relevant to your question (exploratory data analysis)
creates a visualization of the training data that is relevant to your question
performs the classification or regression analysis


Results:

show all the key results that answer your question, using figures and tables
make figures readable in the rendered HTML: label the axes in plain English (with units), include a legend when there is more than one colour or group, use a text size people can read, and avoid overplotting (e.g., with transparency)
keep tables clean: show the rows and columns that matter, with clear column names. Don’t dump a giant data frame.
give every figure and table a number and a caption (it’s ok to manually write down the figure/table number and caption for now, you do not need to use Quarto syntax for this yet), and refer to them in the text
double-check that what you say about the results matches what the figures and tables show

Discussion:

summarize what you found, and link it back to the question you asked
discuss what the findings mean in the real-world context of the problem (the domain)
discuss whether this is what you expected to find
discuss the assumptions and limitations of your methods and findings
discuss what impact such findings could have
discuss what future questions this could lead to

References:

at least 4 citations relevant to the project, including the data set (format is your choice, just be consistent across the references)
every reference in the list should be cited somewhere in the text
references should be actual peer-reviewed publications or reputable sources, not AI hallucinations!


A few writing rules that apply to the whole report:

Write in full sentences. Point form is OK in a few places, but most of your report should be paragraphs.
Don’t use code-style variable names in your writing. Write “flipper length”, not flipper_length_mm.
Spell out acronyms the first time you use them.
Proofread for spelling and grammar before you submit.

The analysis can be performed in either R or Python. The restrictions on the analysis methods and programming language are put in place to ensure that all group members can contribute equally to the project.
The data for the project should be publicly available, and clearly licensed to be shared and used openly on the internet. We strongly suggest you avoid using data sets where authentication is needed for access (e.g., Kaggle) as this adds another layer of complexity when making these projects reproducible. If you do use one, your README must walk the reader through every step of getting and setting up the API token.

Possible data set sources

City of Vancouver Open Data Portal
BC Data Catalogue
Government of Canada open data
GitHub repo of awesome public datasets
UCI Machine Learning Repository: Data Sets
tidytuesday data set
Google Data set search engine
fivethirtyeight R package (if you use this, see the note below!)

Note: if you choose a data set from the fivethirtyeight R package, you cannot copy their scientific question, visualizations or methods from the original FiveThirtyEight articles from where the data sets were first reported on. Finally, with the fivethirtyeight R package data sets, we want you to get practice reading them using the read_* functions in R or Python, so please use the versions of the data sets listed here: https://github.com/rudeboybert/fivethirtyeight/tree/master/data-raw



5. Make the computational environment reproducible
For this project, we will eventually be making the computation environment reproducible through containerization with Docker. For milestone 1 however, we will start with using a virtual environment as our first step towards this. Use one of:

uv (Python): Virtual environments: Python + uv (DSCI 521 notes)
renv (R): Virtual environments: R (DSCI 521 notes)







ImportantYour README instructions are worth 5 all-or-nothing points



5 points of this milestone are for the reproducibility of your README instructions: whether someone can follow them to set up your environment and run your analysis. These points are all-or-nothing. If your instructions do not work exactly as you have written them, you will lose all 5 points.
Make sure your instructions work on both Windows and Mac computers. If your team does not have both, work with another team to test them.

text:
Expectations

Everyone should contribute equally to all aspects of the project (e.g., code, writing, project management). This should be evidenced by a roughly equal number of commits, pull request reviews and participation in communication via GitHub issues.
After the repository is set up, each group member should work in a GitHub flow workflow:

create a branch in your team’s repository (not a fork) for each feature or fix
give branches meaningful names that describe the work (e.g., add-eda-plot, not branch1 or alice)
keep each branch small: one independent piece of work, not half the project
open a pull request, and have at least one other teammate review it before it is merged. Don’t push straight to main.

You should be committing to git and pushing to GitHub.com every time you work on this project.
Git commit messages should be meaningful. These will be marked. It’s OK if one or two are less meaningful, but most should be.

Below we list some examples of steps that your current report document can be broken up into. It is not critical you split your code up exaclty as we list below, but you must somehow split your analysis code up into 4, or more, R or Python scripts.

Download/extract data

The output of the first script must be the input of the second, and so on. All scripts should have command line arguments and we expect you to use the click) Python package for parsing command line arguments for Python projects, and the docopt R package for parsing command line arguments for R projects.

A first script that downloads the data from the internet and saves it locally. This should take at least two arguments:

the path to the input file (a URL or a relative local path, such as data/file.csv), as well as
a path/filename where to write the file to and what to call it (e.g., data/cleaned_data.csv).

A second script that reads the data from the first script and performs and data cleaning/pre-processing, transforming, and/or partitioning that needs to happen before exploratory data analysis or modeling takes place. This should take at least two arguments:

a path/filename pointing to the data to be read in
a path/filename pointing to where the cleaned/processed/transformed/partitioned data should live.

A third script which creates exploratory data visualization(s) and table(s) that are useful to help the reader/consumer understand that data set. These analysis artifacts should be written to files. This should take at least two arguments:

a path/filename pointing to the data,

title: Git Cheatsheet
text: Run all of these commands in your terminal, from inside your project folder (except git clone, which creates the folder for you). For the full explanations, see the textbook chapters on Git basics, Git history, Git branches, and merge conflicts.

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
1 The Everyday Workflow







Task
Command




Clone a remote version control repository from GitHub.com to your local computer
git clone <URL>


Check the status of the local version control repository
git status


Add a file to the staging area
git add <FILENAME>


Commit staged files to the version control history
git commit -m "Some relevant message about the changes"


Push changes from the local repository to the remote repository on GitHub.com
git push


Pull changes from the remote repository on GitHub.com to the local repository
git pull


View the version control history
git log



The usual loop is: git pull → edit files → git status → git add → git commit → git push.

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
2 Getting a Repository

git clone <URL> — Copy a remote repository from GitHub.com to your computer

Example: git clone https://github.com/UBC-MDS/DSCI_522_dsci-workflows_students.git

This creates a new folder named after the repository. Use cd <folder_name> to go into it.

Do not clone a repository inside another repository.

git init — Turn the current folder into a new, empty Git repository

Only needed when you start a project locally. If you start on GitHub.com and then git clone, you do not need it.

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
3 Checking the Status

git status — Show which files are modified, staged, or not tracked yet

Run it often, especially before git add and git commit.

git diff — Show the changes you made that are not staged yet

git diff --staged — Show the changes that are staged and will go into the next commit

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
4 Staging and Committing

git add <FILENAME> — Add a file to the staging area

git add <FILE1> <FILE2> — Add several files at once

git add <FOLDER>/ — Add everything in a folder

git add . — Add all changes in the current folder (check git status first so you only stage what you mean to)

git commit -m "Some relevant message about the changes" — Commit the staged files to the version control history

Write a short, specific message that says what changed and why.
Only staged files are committed.

git restore --staged <FILENAME> — Unstage a file (your edits to the file are kept)
git restore <FILENAME> — Discard your unstaged edits to a file and go back to the last commit

⚠️ This cannot be undone.

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
5 Syncing with GitHub

git push — Send your local commits to the remote repository on GitHub.com

First push of a new branch: git push -u origin <BRANCH_NAME> (-u stands for --set-upstream). See the branches section below for the difference between this and git push origin <BRANCH_NAME>.

git pull — Get changes from the remote repository on GitHub.com and merge them into your local repository

Pull before you start working, and before you push, to avoid conflicts.

git fetch — Download the latest changes from GitHub.com without merging them into your files
git remote -v — Show the URL of the remote repository your local repository is connected to

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
6 Viewing the History

git log — View the version control history

Press q to exit the log. Use the arrow keys, b, or the space bar to scroll.

Press / + a search term + Enter to search the log; n / N jump to the next / previous match.

git log -n 3 — Show only the last 3 commits

git log <FILENAME> — Show only the commits that changed this file

git show <COMMIT_ID> — Show the changes made in one commit

The commit ID (also called the commit hash, or SHA) is the long string of letters and numbers after commit in git log. It is a hash of the commit’s contents, so each commit has a unique one.

The first 7 characters (the short SHA) are usually enough: git show 238dbcb








TipJust want a look at the past?



On GitHub.com, click the commits link on the repository’s main page to see the history and commit messages. Click the <> button next to a commit to view the state of the whole repository at that point in time.

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
7 Going Back in Time
Use these in your local repository when you want to run or explore files from the past, or bring a past version of a file into the present.

git checkout <COMMIT_ID> . — Move the whole project (all files and directories) back to the state of that commit

The last . is really important, so don’t forget it!

Example: git checkout 9b4af1d .

The files now look like they did at that commit, so you can explore and run them.

git checkout HEAD . — Go back to the future: return to the most recent commit

HEAD is the nickname for the most recent commit.

Run git log afterwards to check you returned safely.

git checkout <COMMIT_ID> <FILENAME> — Bring back the version of a single file from a past commit

Example: git checkout 5837143 doc/count_report.Rmd

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
8 Branches

git branch — List the local branches (the current one is marked with *)

git branch -v — Also show the SHA and message of the last commit on each branch (-v stands for --verbose)
git branch -a — Also list the branches on the remote

git switch -c <BRANCH_NAME> — Create a new branch and switch to it

Same as git checkout -b <BRANCH_NAME>

Use a descriptive name, e.g. patch-docs for a fix to the documentation.

git switch <BRANCH_NAME> — Switch to an existing branch (no -c, since we are not creating one)

Same as git checkout <BRANCH_NAME>

git fetch --all — Download all changes to all branches from the remote, so you can switch to a branch a collaborator created
git push origin <BRANCH_NAME> — Push the changes on a branch to the remote repository (usually named origin)

This pushes once. Git does not remember the connection, so a plain git push on that branch fails with fatal: The current branch <BRANCH_NAME> has no upstream branch, and you have to type git push origin <BRANCH_NAME> every time.

git push -u origin <BRANCH_NAME> — Push and link your local branch to the remote branch of the same name (-u stands for --set-upstream). After this, plain git push and git pull work on that branch, and git status tells you whether you are ahead of or behind the remote.

You only need -u the first time you push a new branch.

git merge <BRANCH_NAME> — Merge the branch <BRANCH_NAME> into the branch you are currently on

If the same lines were changed in both branches, Git stops with a merge conflict. Open the files with <<<<<<< markers, choose what to keep, then git add and git commit.

git branch -d <BRANCH_NAME> — Delete a local branch that has been merged







TipTypical branch workflow




git switch main and git pull — start from the latest main
git switch -c my-new-feature — create a branch
Edit, git add, git commit (repeat as needed)
git push -u origin my-new-feature — push the branch
Open a pull request on GitHub.com, get it reviewed, and merge it there
git switch main and git pull — bring the merged work back to your computer

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
9 Ignoring Files
.gitignore — A text file in the root of the repository listing files and folders that Git should not track
- One pattern per line, e.g. .venv/, *.log, .DS_Store
- Prepend **/ to a file or folder name (e.g. **/.venv/, **/.DS_Store) to also ignore it in subdirectories anywhere within the repository

2.2 Update .qmd file

2.2.1 Header formatting & table of contents

TODO: Add header formatting to sections (e.g., “Aim”, “Data”, “Methods”, “Results”, “References”) and Quarto configuration so that a table of contents that is automatically generated from the document headers will be created when the document is rendered

We will update the yml header to add table of contents. We will add table of content (toc) with depth 3 for both html and pdf formats. Your yml header at the begining of the file (i.e., qmd_example.qmd) should be updated to look like this:
title: "DSCI 310: Historical Horse Population in Canada"
author: "Tiffany Timbers & Jordan Bourak"
format: html
editor: source
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
  pdf:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
You will format header sections using #, ##, ###, etc. For example, I’ve added the following header sections to the qmd_example.qmd file:
# Aim
...
# Data
...
# Methods
...
# Results
...
# References


2.2.2 References

TODO: Add correctly formatted inline BibTeX references so that a nicely formatted reference list will be present at the end of the document.

You already have a references.bib file in the repository under the reports folder. We will point bibliography to look for references in this file in the yml header as follows:
title: "DSCI 310: Historical Horse Population in Canada"
author: "Tiffany Timbers & Jordan Bourak"
format: html
editor: source
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
  pdf:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
bibliography: references.bib






NoteHigh bug zone: indentation & missing colon:




Quarto’s yaml uses 2 whitespaces to indent the yaml fields (not 4 whitespaces!! not tab!!).
Please use : to separate the field name and the field value.



Let’s render what we have so far to see the result. In your terminal, please run the following commands:
# go to the reports directory if you are in the root directory
cd reports

# render the html file
quarto render qmd_example.qmd






NoteNo references listed in the rendered report??



You will notice that no references are listed in the rendered pdf or html file. This is because we have not added in-text citations to the .qmd file. You can list as many BibTex references as you want in your references.bib file. However, only the references that are cited in the .qmd file will be listed in the rendered pdf or html file under “References” section.


Let’s add in-text citations to the .qmd file. We will use the [@reference_key] syntax (or [@reference_key1; @reference_key2] when you have more than 1 reference) to cite references. Please note the reference_key is the first phrase after { in the BibTex entry. For example, for this entry in the references.bib file:
@Manual{click,
    title           = {Click Python Package},
    author          = {Pallets Team},
    year            = {2020},
    url             = {https://click.palletsprojects.com/},
}
The reference_key is click. We will use [@click] to cite this reference in the .qmd file.
For example, I’ve added the following in-text citations to the .qmd file. Please complete all other in-text citations yourself:
Horse population data were sourced from the 
[Government of Canada's Open Data website](http://open.canada.ca/en/open-data) [@horses1; @horses2]...


2.2.3 Figure formatting

TODO: Edit the figure formatting so that Quarto:

automatically numbers them
has a label for easy cross referencing
controls the figure sizes so the figures are not too big (in particular the second figure in the report should be only 60-70% of the default width)


We use the syntax ![description](relative/path/to/figure.png){#fig-label width=950%} to format the figure. For example, I’ve added the following figure to the .qmd file, and I use @fig-label to refer to it in the text. This will be rendered as Figure 1 in the rendered pdf or html file. You will do so for both Figure 1 + 2.
# Results

![Horse populations for all provinces in Canada from 1906 - 1972.](../results/horse_pops_plot.png){#fig-horse-pop width=60%}

We can see from @fig-horse-pop that Ontario, Saskatchewan and Alberta 






NoteHigh bug zone: Pay attention to using fig-label




You have to name your figure with starting with a fig prefix (sorry for my mistakes in class!).
You have to use - instead of _ in the figure label.
Example: fig-horse-pop instead of horse_pop.





2.2.4 Table formatting

TODO: add a table description argument so that they are automatically numbered by Quarto and use cross referencing to link to the table if/when it is discussed in the text

We use the syntax below inside of python code block to format the table:
#| label: tbl-label
#| tbl-cap: Table description
For example, I’ve added the following table to the .qmd file. @tbl-horse-sd will be rendered as Table 1 in the rendered pdf or html file.
We present the standard deviations in @tbl-horse-sd.

```\{python}
#| label: tbl-horse-sd
#| tbl-cap: Standard deviation of historical (1906-1972) horse populations for each Canadian province.

horses_sd_table = pd.read_csv("../results/horses_sd.csv")
largest_sd = horses_sd_table['Province'].values[0]
Markdown(horses_sd_table.to_markdown(index = False))
```






NoteHigh bug zone: Pay attention to using tbl-label




You have to name your table with starting with a tbl prefix (sorry for my mistakes in class!).
You have to use - instead of _ in the table label.
Example: tbl-horse-sd instead of horse_sd.





2.2.5 Cross-referencing

TODO: Edit the narrative so it uses cross-referencing to refer to the figures and tables instead of having their reference hardcode the figure and table numbers.

In the steps above, we have already used cross-referencing to refer to the figures and tables (e.g., @fig-horse-pop and @tbl-horse-sd).


2.2.6 Inline Quarto code

TODO: replace the ??? in the Quarto report narrative text with inline Quarto code, so that the text will be automatically updated with the correct value

We use the syntax below to do inline Quarto code. It will execute the python / R code inside of the code block and resulting value will be displayed in the text.
`{python} <python_code>`
For example, I’ve added the following inline Quarto code (i.e., {python} largest_sd) to the .qmd file:
```\{python}

#| tbl-cap: Standard deviation of historical (1906-1972) horse populations for each Canadian province.


horses_sd_table = pd.read_csv("../results/horses_sd.csv")
largest_sd = horses_sd_table['Province'].values[0]
Markdown(horses_sd_table.to_markdown(index = False))
```

...

In @fig-horse-largest we zoom in and look at the province of `{python} largest_sd`, which had the largest spread of values in terms of standard deviation.

2.2.8 GitHub Pages

TODO: (optional/bonus) Turn on GitHub pages so that it serves up the docs directory so that the report is viewable on the web.

At the root directoy of your repository, please create a new file called _quarto.yml and add the following content:
project:
  type: website
  output-dir: docs
This file will tell Quarto to output the rendered report to the docs folder, as a website.
Also create an empty file called .nojekyll at the root directory of your repository:
touch .nojekyll
Quarto copies it into the docs folder every time you render, and it tells GitHub Pages to serve your files exactly as they are (see Turning off Jekyll with .nojekyll in the DSCI 521 notes).
Then, at the root directoy of your repository, please run the following command to render the report in the terminal:
quarto render
You will see that the rendered report is now all in the docs folder. There is a index.html file in the docs folder, you can open it in your browser to view the report.
Confirm that .nojekyll is in docs, the folder GitHub Pages publishes from. ls hides files whose names start with a dot, so add -a:
ls -a docs
You should see .nojekyll in the list.






NoteNo image showing in Jupyter lab??



It is normal to not see figures being rendered inside of Jupyter lab. You will need to go to local folder, and double click on the index.html file to view the report in a browser.
